lessons.title: One God, the Gurus and Sikh Beliefs about Humanity

before.content_html:
Ik Onkar — There Is Only One God

At the very heart of Sikhism is an absolute and uncompromising belief in one God. The symbol Ik Onkar (‘There is only one God’) opens the Mool Mantar, the foundational statement of Sikh belief found at the very beginning of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scriptures. The Mool Mantar was composed by Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, and describes the nature of God: God is one (ik onkar), truth (satnam), the creator (kartapurkh), without fear (nirbhau), without hate (nirvair), timeless (akal), beyond birth and death (ajooni), self-existent (saibhang), and known through the Guru’s grace.

Key Fact

The Mool Mantar, opening the Guru Granth Sahib at page 1, is the foundational Sikh statement of faith. It teaches that God is one, true, the creator, without fear or hatred, eternal, beyond birth and death, and known through grace. Ik Onkar encapsulates the entire Sikh theological world view in two syllables.

God as Immanent, All-Pervading and Self-Revealing

Sikhs believe God is immanent — present within creation and within every person. God is not remote or absent but actively present in all things. The Guru Granth Sahib (page 1) teaches this from the very outset: God permeates all creation. Unlike traditions that emphasise God as wholly ‘other’ and separate from the world, Sikhism holds that God is found within the self and in all of existence.

God is also self-revealing: humans cannot discover God through their own unaided effort or reason alone. God reveals himself through grace (nadar) and through the Guru. The concept of the Guru is therefore central — it refers not only to the human Gurus of Sikh history but ultimately to the divine Word or wisdom of God itself. The Guru Granth Sahib (page 294) describes God as personal, as creator and as Guru — one who teaches and guides. This makes God in Sikhism both transcendent (beyond human comprehension) and immanent (intimately present within all).

Sikhism uses many names to describe the one God, reflecting the richness of divine qualities. Among the most important are:

Waheguru (‘Wonderful Lord’) — the most commonly used Sikh name for God in devotional practice. It expresses awe and wonder at the divine. Sikhs use ‘Waheguru’ as a meditation name, repeating it to focus the mind on God.

Satnam (‘True Name’) — found in the Mool Mantar, emphasising God’s nature as truth. Akal Purakh (‘Timeless Being’) — emphasising God’s eternal existence beyond time and death. Kartapurkh (‘Creator Being’) — emphasising God as the active creator and sustainer of all existence. These names come from the Guru Granth Sahib and are used in prayer and meditation.

The Role and Purpose of Humanity — Mukti

Sikhism teaches that the human life is a precious and rare opportunity. Sikhs believe in karma and rebirth: the soul passes through many forms of existence before reaching human life. Human birth is the crucial stage in which the soul can choose to turn towards God. The Guru Granth Sahib (pages 2 and 11) teaches that without God’s name, people waste this precious human existence wandering in spiritual ignorance.

Mukti (also written moksha) is the Sikh term for liberation — the ultimate spiritual goal. It is understood as the union of the soul with God, ending the cycle of rebirth. However, Sikhism’s vision of liberation is different from some Hindu interpretations: in Sikhism, the liberated soul does not dissolve into God without identity, but continues in a state of loving union and service to God. The Guru Granth Sahib (page 43) teaches of the joy of this union.

Key Fact

Mukti (liberation) is achieved through simran — meditating on God’s name (Nam). The Guru Granth Sahib (page 125) teaches that by meditating on God’s name, a person becomes a gurmukh (one who faces the Guru) rather than a manmukh (one who is self-centred). The gurmukh lives in harmony with God’s will; the manmukh is driven by ego and desire.

Gurmukh and Manmukh

One of Sikhism’s central distinctions is between the gurmukh (one who faces the Guru / God-centred person) and the manmukh (one who is self-centred or ego-driven). The gurmukh meditates on God’s name, performs sewa (selfless service), lives honestly and treats all people as equal. The manmukh, by contrast, is trapped in haumai (ego or self-centredness) — the primary barrier to mukti in Sikh teaching. Haumai leads to attachment to the material world, pride and self-interest, which generate bad karma and further rebirth. The Guru Granth Sahib (page 125) teaches that the gurmukh is absorbed in God’s name and attains liberation.

The Sikh Gurus strongly emphasised that spiritual life should be lived within the world, not withdrawn from it. This makes Sikhism distinctively a householder religion. The ideal Sikh life combines three core principles: Nam Japna (meditating on God’s name), Kirat Karni (honest labour — earning one’s living through honourable work) and Vand Chakna (sharing with others — contributing a portion of one’s income or time to the community). Together these principles shape a life of spiritual devotion embedded in everyday responsibility.

Family life is central to Sikh teaching. Unlike traditions that regard celibacy or withdrawal from the world as the highest path, the Sikh Gurus taught that God can be found within family life, work and community. The family is considered the basic unit of Sikh spiritual community, and children are to be raised in Sikh teaching from birth. This emphasis on family life means Sikhism presents a vision of holiness that is accessible to all, not only to monks or ascetics.

lessons.title: Worship in the Gurdwara, Langar and Sikh Initiation

before.content_html:
The Gurdwara — The Sikh Place of Worship

Gurdwara means ‘gateway to the Guru’. Any building where the Guru Granth Sahib is permanently installed and Sikhs gather for worship can be a gurdwara. The gurdwara has several key architectural and functional features that reflect Sikh values of equality, community and devotion to God.

The most important feature of any gurdwara is the Darbar Sahib (Presence Chamber) — the main hall of worship where the Guru Granth Sahib is kept on a raised platform (takht or throne) beneath a canopy (palki). The Guru Granth Sahib is treated as the living Guru: it is brought in a ceremonial procession in the morning, read aloud throughout the day, and put to rest at night. Outside the gurdwara flies the Nishan Sahib — the triangular Sikh flag carrying the Khanda symbol. The flag signals to all that this is a gurdwara and that all are welcome.

Key Fact

Key features of a gurdwara include: the Darbar Sahib (prayer hall with the Guru Granth Sahib on the takht), the Nishan Sahib (flag outside), the langar hall (community kitchen and dining area), and a room for the Guru Granth Sahib to ‘rest’ at night. All these features embody Sikh values: devotion, equality, welcome and service.

The Guru Granth Sahib in Worship

The Guru Granth Sahib is central to every act of Sikh worship. It is not simply a book: Sikhs regard it as the eleventh and final Guru — the living Word of God. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth human Guru, declared before his death in 1708 that there would be no further human Gurus; henceforth the scripture itself would serve as Guru for the Sikh community. This is one of the most distinctive aspects of Sikhism — a living scripture that functions as a living teacher.

In worship, the Guru Granth Sahib is read aloud and its words are sung in a distinctive style called kirtan. Professional musicians and readers called ragis sing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib to classical Indian musical modes (ragas). The congregation sits on the floor in front of the Guru Granth Sahib — everyone at the same level, reflecting the Sikh commitment to equality. Worshippers bow before the scripture and pass in front of it barefoot and with heads covered as a mark of respect.

The granthi is the person who reads and cares for the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara. The granthi is not a priest in the sense of having special spiritual authority — any Sikh who can read the Guru Granth Sahib in its original Gurmukhi script can perform this role. This is theologically significant: Sikhism has no clergy as an intermediary between God and the worshipper. Both men and women can serve as granthis, reflecting Sikh teaching on equality.

A Sikh service typically ends with the Ardas — a formal communal prayer recited standing, with hands clasped, petitioning God for the welfare of the community and all humanity. After the Ardas, a random passage is opened from the Guru Granth Sahib — this is called the Hukamnama (divine command) — and the opening verse is read aloud as God’s guidance for the day. The service concludes with the distribution of karah prashad.

Karah Prashad and Langar

Karah prashad is a sacred sweet food made from equal quantities of flour, sugar and ghee (clarified butter), prepared with prayers. It is distributed to everyone present at the end of worship — regardless of religion, caste or background. The equal distribution of karah prashad symbolises the Sikh belief in the equality of all people before God. No one is turned away and every portion is equal.

The langar is the community kitchen and free vegetarian meal served in every gurdwara. It was introduced by Guru Nanak and developed by subsequent Gurus as a practical expression of Sikh values. The langar meal is prepared and served by volunteers as an act of sewa (selfless service). Its significance is profound: by eating together, sitting on the floor in rows, people of all backgrounds, faiths and social positions are made equal. Historically, this was a radical challenge to caste-based dining restrictions. The Guru Granth Sahib (page 349) affirms the value of seva and the community practice of sharing food together.

Key Fact

Both karah prashad (sacred food shared equally) and langar (free community meal for all) express the Sikh belief that all people are equal before God. Both challenge caste distinctions: sharing food with people of all backgrounds was historically radical. The Guru Granth Sahib (p.349) connects langar to sewa and equality.

Naming a Sikh Child

When a Sikh baby is born, the family brings the child to the gurdwara for a naming ceremony. A passage is chosen at random from the Guru Granth Sahib (Hukamnama), and the baby is given a name beginning with the first letter of the first word of the passage. This is called Naam Karan. The baby’s name connects them to the Guru Granth Sahib from the very first days of life. All Sikh boys receive the additional name Singh (meaning ‘lion’) and all girls receive the name Kaur (meaning ‘princess’ or ‘princess of the royal court’). These names were given by Guru Gobind Singh to abolish caste-based surnames, which would reveal a person’s birth status. By giving all Sikhs the same names, the Gurus declared the equality of all.

The Amrit Sanskar — Sikh Initiation

The Amrit Sanskar (also called the Khalsa initiation or Amrit Ceremony) is the ceremony in which a Sikh formally joins the Khalsa — the community of initiated Sikhs. It was established by Guru Gobind Singh at Vaisakhi in 1699. The ceremony involves:

The ceremony takes place in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and five initiated Sikhs (the Panj Pyare — ‘Five Beloved Ones’, representing the original five Sikhs who volunteered their lives to Guru Gobind Singh in 1699). Amrit — sacred sugar water stirred with a double-edged sword (khanda) while hymns are recited — is prepared. The initiate drinks amrit five times, has it sprinkled on their eyes and hair, and repeats the Mool Mantar five times. They commit to observe the Sikh code of conduct (Rehat Maryada) and to wear the Five Ks (Panj Kakars).

The Five Ks are: Kesh (uncut hair — symbolising acceptance of God’s will and distinctively Sikh identity); Kangha (a small wooden comb kept in the hair — symbolising cleanliness and spiritual discipline); Kara (a steel bracelet on the right wrist — symbolising eternal God, who has no beginning or end, and the Sikh’s commitment to righteous action); Kachera (cotton shorts — symbolising chastity and moral restraint); and Kirpan (a steel sword — symbolising the duty to defend the weak and fight injustice). Together the Five Ks make a Khalsa Sikh visually identifiable and connect every initiated Sikh to the same community of commitment.

Not all Sikhs take Amrit. Those who have not yet done so are called Sahajdhari Sikhs — those on the path but who have not yet undergone initiation. Sikhism recognises both groups as genuine members of the Sikh faith. This reflects an important diversity within the Sikh community that students should acknowledge when answering exam questions about Sikh identity.
before.exam_tip_html: For questions about Sikh worship or the Five Ks, always explain the significance behind each feature rather than just listing them. For example, don’t just say ‘Sikhs wear the Kara’ — explain it is a steel bracelet symbolising God’s eternity (no beginning or end) and the Sikh’s commitment to righteous action. For evaluation questions about the importance of langar, note that not all Sikhs eat langar daily but it remains a central Sikh institution — this shows you understand the diversity of practice, which examiners reward in higher-mark responses.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of a gurdwara.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: Darbar Sahib (main prayer hall with Guru Granth Sahib on the takht/throne); Nishan Sahib (Sikh flag outside); langar hall (community kitchen and dining room); room for the Guru Granth Sahib to rest; washing/shoe removal area at entrance.

Two marks for: the community kitchen and free vegetarian meal served in every gurdwara, open to all regardless of religion, caste, gender or background, expressing Sikh equality and sewa. One mark for: 'free food at the gurdwara' or 'community kitchen' without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe the features and importance of the langar in the gurdwara.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Features: free vegetarian meal; prepared and served by volunteers as sewa; open to all regardless of background; everyone sits together on the floor in rows; introduced by Guru Nanak. Importance: expresses Sikh equality (all eat together); challenges caste dining restrictions; embodies sewa; Guru Granth Sahib (p.349) connects langar to selfless service. Secure: Clear description with features and some importance. Developing: Describes langar as a free meal without much detail on importance. Emerging: Brief mention of a free meal.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Amrit Sanskar ceremony influences the life of a Khalsa Sikh.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the Amrit ceremony (drinking amrit, Panj Pyare present, commitment to Rehat Maryada); influence: wearing the Five Ks as visible identity; commitment to the Sikh code of conduct; belonging to the Khalsa community; accepting names Singh/Kaur. Shows how the ceremony shapes daily practice and Sikh identity. Secure: Clear explanation of ceremony and at least two developed influences. Developing: Basic description of ceremony; limited influence. Emerging: Mentions the Five Ks without connecting to the ceremony.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Guru Granth Sahib is central to Sikh worship.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Way 1: The Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru — Guru Gobind Singh declared it the eternal Guru in 1708; it is installed on a throne, carried in procession, and read aloud; the Hukamnama provides daily guidance. Way 2: The Guru Granth Sahib structures community worship — kirtan (hymn-singing), Ardas, karah prashad all centre on the scripture; GGS p.349 affirms the value of community worship and service. Secure: Two ways explained with at least one textual reference. Developing: Two ways stated; underdeveloped or lacking a source. Emerging: One way with little development.

practice_questions.text:
'Wearing the Five Ks is the most important way a Sikh shows their faith.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees: the Five Ks are a visible external commitment to the Khalsa; they mark a Sikh as distinctive; wearing Kesh and Kirpan can involve real social challenges in a non-Sikh society; they were given by Guru Gobind Singh as part of the Amrit Sanskar. Disagrees: not all Sikhs take Amrit or wear the Five Ks (Sahajdhari Sikhs); the Guru Granth Sahib teaches that inner devotion (simran, sewa) matters more than external forms; Guru Nanak criticised empty ritual; daily practices of Nam Japna, Kirat Karni and Vand Chakna may be more day-to-day expressions of faith. Non-religious view: a Humanist would argue that commitment to equality and service (langar, sewa) expresses values more meaningfully than dress. Justified conclusion. Secure: Two developed arguments with at least one source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides; limited evaluation. Emerging: Descriptive or one-sided.

before.content_html:
Authority in Sikhism

Sikhism was shaped by ten human Gurus, beginning with Guru Nanak (1469–1539) and ending with Guru Gobind Singh (1666–1708). Before his death, Guru Gobind Singh declared that there would be no eleventh human Guru. Instead, authority passed permanently to the sacred scripture: the Guru Granth Sahib. This means that for Sikhs today, the scripture is not merely a holy book; it is treated as a living presence and the source of all spiritual guidance.

In the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib is placed on a raised platform called the Takht, covered in fine cloth, and fanned with a chauri (a ceremonial whisk) as a sign of royal honour. Worshippers bow before it when entering. A granthi reads from it at every service. Before the scripture is put to rest at night, it is ceremonially processed and wrapped — as a living being would be treated during sleep. This treatment communicates a central Sikh belief: the word of God, as revealed through the Gurus, is eternally present and active in the world.

Key Fact

Guru Gobind Singh (the tenth Guru) declared the Guru Granth Sahib to be the eternal, living Guru of the Sikhs in 1708. No human Guru has succeeded him. The scripture now holds final spiritual authority for all Sikhs.

The Khalsa

In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa at Vaisakhi. The story tells that he called for volunteers willing to give their lives for their faith. Five men — the Panj Pyare (‘Five Beloved’) — stepped forward. Guru Gobind Singh baptised them with Amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword) and they became the first members of the Khalsa. The Guru then asked them to initiate him in return, showing that all were equal before God.

Members of the Khalsa commit to wearing the Five Ks (panj kakars) — kesh (uncut hair), kangha (small comb), kara (steel bracelet), kaccha (modest undergarment) and kirpan (a small sword representing the duty to defend the oppressed). Khalsa Sikhs also take on the names Singh (‘lion’) for men and Kaur (‘princess’) for women, abolishing caste-based surnames. The Khalsa is not only a religious community; it represents Sikh identity, courage and commitment to justice.

Not all Sikhs take Amrit initiation. Sahajdhari Sikhs are those who follow Sikh teachings and may observe some or all of the Five Ks but have not undergone the formal Amrit ceremony. The Khalsa represents the ideal of full commitment, but Sikh teaching emphasises that God’s grace is available to all who sincerely seek it. Both Khalsa and non-Khalsa Sikhs are part of the Sikh community (the Sangat) and are equally welcome in the gurdwara.

Equality: A Core Sikh Teaching

Equality is not peripheral to Sikhism — it is central. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that all people are formed from the same divine light and that distinctions of caste, gender, religion or status have no spiritual significance. The Gurus condemned the caste system explicitly. The scripture describes all humanity as ‘born from the same clay’ (Guru Granth Sahib, pauri 349), affirming that no person is superior by birth.

This teaching of equality has three practical expressions in Sikh life: the sangat (the equal congregation, where all sit together regardless of background), the langar (the community kitchen where all eat together, sitting on the floor as equals), and the principle of sewa (selfless service). These are not optional extras; they are expressions of what the Gurus taught about the oneness of humanity before God.

Key Fact

The Guru Granth Sahib (page 349) affirms the equality of all people and the condemnation of caste. In practice, the langar (community kitchen) at every gurdwara serves free food to all visitors — regardless of faith, background or wealth — as a visible expression of this teaching.

Male–Female Equality

The Gurus also taught the equality of women and men. Women are permitted to read from the Guru Granth Sahib (as granthis), lead prayers, take part in all aspects of gurdwara life and receive Amrit initiation as full members of the Khalsa. The scripture affirms that women are equally capable of spiritual achievement. In many communities, women take an active leadership role, and Sikh festivals and rites of passage apply equally to both sexes.

Sikh marriage (Anand Karaj, ‘ceremony of bliss’) takes place in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. The ceremony centres on the Lavan — four hymns written by Guru Ram Das (Guru Granth Sahib, pages 773–774). As each hymn is read aloud and sung by the ragis (musicians), the couple circles the Guru Granth Sahib, the man leading and the woman following closely. The four circlings (pheras) represent the couple’s spiritual journey together toward God. The ceremony is not a legal contract between two families; it is a spiritual union witnessed by the Guru Granth Sahib and the Sangat.

Sikh funerals (Antam Sanskar) also reflect core beliefs. The body is cremated, symbolising the soul’s release from the cycle of rebirth (samsara). Readings from the Guru Granth Sahib and singing of the Kirtan Sohila (the night prayer) accompany the ceremony. Cremation reflects the belief that the physical body returns to the elements while the soul continues its journey toward mukti (liberation).

Gurpurbs: Festivals Honouring the Gurus

Gurpurbs are holy days commemorating the Gurus. The most widely celebrated are the birthdays of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh and the martyrdom of Guru Arjan. Guru Arjan was tortured and killed in 1606 by the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, making him the first Sikh martyr. His death is remembered each year as a witness to the Sikh commitment to truth and justice.

Gurpurbs are celebrated with an Akhand Path (a continuous, uninterrupted reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib over approximately 48 hours), Nagar Kirtan (a procession through the streets singing hymns), and the distribution of karah prashad (a sweet, sanctified food given to all). These practices reinforce the Sikh values of community, equality and devotion.

Vaisakhi (also Baisakhi) is the most important Sikh festival. Celebrated on 13 or 14 April, it commemorates the founding of the Khalsa in 1699. Vaisakhi is celebrated with processions, kirtan singing, prayers and new Amrit initiations into the Khalsa. It is both a harvest festival and a deeply religious occasion marking the birth of the Sikh community as Guru Gobind Singh envisioned it.

Sikhs also celebrate Diwali, but their reasons differ from the Hindu festival. Sikhs celebrate Diwali as Bandi Chhor Divas (‘Day of Liberation’), commemorating the release of Guru Hargobind (the sixth Guru) from Gwalior Fort, where he had been imprisoned by Emperor Jahangir. According to tradition, Guru Hargobind refused to leave unless 52 Hindu princes imprisoned alongside him were also released. They were, and the Guru returned in triumph to Amritsar. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) was lit with lamps to welcome him — hence the association with lights.

Hola Mohalla is celebrated the day after Holi and was introduced by Guru Gobind Singh as a Sikh alternative. It involves martial arts displays, poetry competitions and music, and is associated with the spirit of the Khalsa. Today it is most famously celebrated at Anandpur Sahib.

practice_questions.text: Give two gurpurbs celebrated in Sikhism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: Birthday of Guru Nanak / Birthday of Guru Gobind Singh / Martyrdom of Guru Arjan. [2 marks]

The four wedding hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib (pages 773–774) recited and sung during the Sikh marriage ceremony, around which the couple circles four times. [2 marks — 1 for identification, 1 for explanation of significance]

practice_questions.text: Describe Sikh beliefs and teachings about equality.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed account with two or more distinct points, specific reference to Guru Granth Sahib 349 or Khalsa founding, plus explanation of why equality matters in Sikh theology (all from same clay / divine light in all).
Secure: Two clear points (e.g. langar, caste condemnation) with some explanation of significance.
Developing: One or two points, mostly descriptive, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification of one feature only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the celebration of Vaisakhi influences the lives of Sikhs today.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed points showing influence (e.g. new Amrit initiations strengthen Khalsa identity; Nagar Kirtan processions bring community together and demonstrate faith publicly) each linked to the historical founding in 1699.
Secure: Two points with some explanation of influence.
Developing: One developed point or two simple points.
Emerging: Simple statement about Vaisakhi without explaining influence.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Sikh beliefs about the authority of the Guru Granth Sahib.
Refer to Sikh teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct beliefs each developed with a source of authority (e.g. treated as living Guru — chauri, Takht, ceremonial respect; eternal word of God replacing human Gurus — Guru Gobind Singh's declaration in 1708) and explained in terms of why it matters to Sikhs.
Secure: Two beliefs, each with reference to teaching and some development.
Developing: One well-developed belief or two briefly stated.
Emerging: One or two simple points, no source of authority.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important Sikh teaching is the equality of all people.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Guru Granth Sahib 349 explicitly condemns caste — 'born from same clay' — placing equality at the heart of revealed teaching.
• Practical institutions (langar, sangat, sewa) express equality in everyday Sikh life, making it more than abstract doctrine.
• Guru Gobind Singh's Khalsa abolished caste-based names, giving equality structural expression in Sikh identity.
• Non-religious view: humanist thinkers argue equality is the foundation of human dignity independently of any religious framework.
Arguments against:
• The authority of the Guru Granth Sahib as living Guru could be considered more fundamental — without this source of authority, equality teachings lose their divine grounding.
• Belief in one God (Waheguru) and the goal of mukti (union with God) might be argued as the theological foundation that makes all other teachings, including equality, possible.
• The Khalsa's five commitments (Five Ks) could be seen as the defining Sikh teaching because they involve active, visible commitment, not just belief.
Conclusion: A justified personal judgement weighing which teaching is most fundamental.
Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument with named sources, non-religious view included, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, conclusion present.
Developing: One side stronger than other, limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided or no conclusion.
